::: {.why}
A point estimate with no interval is what let the last twenty years of published backtests happen, and you are about to make it impossible for yourself to report one.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Return a Sharpe ratio with its standard error and confidence interval from one function call.
- Show your interval is correctly calibrated by simulation, not by assertion.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Extend qlib/stats.py: have `sharpe()` return the estimate, its standard error from yesterday's formula, the sample size, and a 95 percent interval. Make the interval the default thing that gets printed, so reporting a bare number takes deliberate effort.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Write tests/test_stats.py with a coverage test: simulate 2,000 series at a known true Sharpe, compute the interval for each, and assert the empirical coverage is within sampling error of 95 percent. This is the test that catches the annualisation factor being applied to the standard error in the wrong place, which is the standard bug here.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The performance layer now reports intervals by default and has a coverage test behind them. From here, any strategy result in this course that appears without an interval is a bug rather than a style choice.
:::
